keys.why: What this course calls the folder holding one page per curriculum expectation. Declared by every payload and skeleton manifest and carried here at creation; the build tries it FIRST and only then falls back to scanning for a top-level folder whose name contains 'curriculum'. The fallback is still the real path for a course made from scratch, which has no manifest to declare anything — but a course whose folder is called something else entirely would otherwise never have its map built at all.

Which per-section folder holds this course's class pages. ABSENT or unmatched falls back to the old GUESS — the first per-section folder whose name contains 'class' (case-insensitive), else the first entry, else the literal 'All Classes' — which is what every course made before this key existed relies on. The key exists because the guess quietly decided what a teacher was allowed to CALL this folder: somebody whose vocabulary is 'Thread 2, Day 3' would sensibly call it 'All Days', and under the guess alone that folder is not found, so the first per-section folder is used instead and the curriculum map counts the wrong pages. The map does not FAIL when that happens — it falls back to counting every published page, which is a wrong map that reports success. Written by both wizards at creation, and MATERIALISED by a rename: renaming the class folder writes this key even on a course that never had one, because a rename is the one moment Plantoir witnesses the change. Compared case-insensitively, and the LIST's spelling wins over the key's, because everything downstream builds file paths from the answer.

What this course calls the first half of a class page's name — “Unit 2, Day 3”, or “Module 2, Day 3”. ABSENT means “Unit”, which is what every course made before this key existed says; empty means the same, and the two are deliberately NOT distinguished the way graded_folders distinguishes them, because there is no sensible reading of “the teacher cleared the word” and a course whose class pages had no name could not be built. Until 2026-09-01 the word was a structural assumption rather than a preference: the regex deciding whether a page is a class page, the page the next-class button writes, and the curriculum map's idea of what a course TEACHES all had it built in — so a teacher who renamed the pages in Obsidian lost every feature that recognises a class page, and the coverage map does not FAIL when it finds none, it falls back to counting every published page, which is a wrong map that reports success. Chosen at course creation and nowhere else: the ready-made pages are poured in the teacher's word rather than renamed afterwards. Renaming a course ALREADY IN USE is a different and far more dangerous piece of work — not because of scale (a ready-made course holds 84–87 class pages — 42 for the two half-credit courses, CHV2O and GLC2O; the 3,172 figure quoted elsewhere is the total across all 38 payloads), but because it means rewriting every wikilink pointing at every renamed page across every section and shared folder, and a half-finished pass leaves a broken site with no way back and no undo. “Day” is deliberately not configurable — a teacher who says “Thread” almost certainly still says “Day 3”.

Folder names whose contents count for marks — what makes an expectation 'assessed' on the Curriculum Coverage map. ABSENT (not `[]`) for every course that has not been asked, and that distinction is load-bearing: absent means the historical rule applies (any folder whose name contains 'task'), while `[]` means the teacher deliberately cleared the list. Seeding an existing course with ["Tasks"] would silently drop folders the old substring rule counted, such as the skeletons' "Thinking Tasks". See shared-rules.json -> gradedFolders.

Extra destinations a course ALSO publishes to, beyond `deploy_target` (the primary) — for redundancy against one host having a bad day. `type` uses the same spellings as `deploy_target`; `path` is only present for `local_folder` entries. ABSENT (not `[]`) for every course that has not opted in, so a course nobody has touched writes the exact same file it always has.

keys.type: object with keys 'shared' (array of strings) and/or 'per_section' (array of strings)
keys.why: Names of folders or files excluded from previews and deploys, separated by scope. Keyed by scope ('shared' and/or 'per_section') to match the config's structure. Course-wide within a scope. ABSENT (not `{}`) when nothing is excluded.

keys.type: per-section map of (per-destination-type map of strings), e.g. custom_domains.sections.section1.netlify
keys.why: Keyed by destination TYPE (`netlify`, `cloudflare_pages` — never `local_folder`, which has no domain concept), not just by section, because a course can publish to more than one destination at once and a domain meant for one must never be applied to another's own link. An OLDER shape — `custom_domains.sections.sectionN` as a bare string, written before a course could have more than one destination — is still read: as the domain for whichever destination is currently `deploy_target` (the primary), and invisible to every other type. Setting a domain for a second destination migrates a bare string it finds into the new shape rather than discarding it.
EMPTY means Netlify, and that is not an oversight: every course written before the other destinations existed has no key at all, and must keep working.

Whether clicking a folder in the site's explorer expands it rather than navigating. Read by `setup_course.py` and baked into Explorer.tsx by `build_site.py` — so this is a key the PYTHON acts on, and an app that never writes it leaves the teacher's choice unrecorded. Found missing from this contract by the count check on its first run, which is what that check is for.
Folders and files kept out of the built site.
The timetable sections a teacher actually teaches — not 1...N. A teacher with sections 2 and 5 has exactly those.
Absent means TRUE — the 'S1' marker shows unless a teacher turns it off.

courseConfigKeys.note: `courses/<CODE>/course_config.json`. Written by the wizard and the settings form, read by both apps AND by `scripts/*.py` — so a key spelled differently on one platform is not a disagreement between two apps, it is a setting the site build silently ignores. Nested keys are per-section maps: `{"sections": {"section1": <value>}}`. The keys fall into TWO groups, and a first draft of this contract only had the first: the settings form round-trips most of them, while a handful are written ONCE by the wizard and read back by `setup_course.py` as the defaults for its own questions. Missing the second group means a teacher on one platform is asked a question the other platform answers for them.

rules.detail: Read the documented default and carry on.
rules.rule: An ABSENT key is not an error
rules.why: Courses created by older versions are missing keys that exist today, and they must open without complaint.

rules.detail: Read the file, change what the teacher changed, write the rest back untouched.
rules.rule: Keys a platform does not understand are PRESERVED
rules.why: The two apps ship at different times. A course saved by the newer one must not lose its settings when opened by the older, and a key dropped this way is invisible until a teacher notices their footer has gone.

keys.requirement: BOTH apps ask the teacher and write the answer. Decided 2026-08-16: Windows matches macOS.
keys.why: Whether a course with no ready-made payload starts from its subject's SKELETON — folders that suit the subject, four units of class pages to rename, placeholders saying what belongs where — or from nothing. Around 1,900 course codes have a skeleton and no payload, so this is the question most teachers actually meet. Both apps write `hasSkeleton(code) && teacherSaidYes`. (Windows did not write it at all until 2026-09-07, so for three weeks the Python took its own default of TRUE and a Windows teacher could not decline.)
Whether one of the 37 ready-made courses is poured in. Written as `hasContent(code) && teacherSaidYes`, so a stale true can never mean anything.
Whether the payload's Curriculum folder comes with it.

wizardAnswerKeys.note: Written by the WIZARD at course creation, not by the settings form. `setup_course.py` reads each as the default for a question it would otherwise ask — so an app that omits one leaves the Python to take its own default, and the teacher never gets the choice. All three are the TEACHER's answers, on both platforms: the wizard asks, the app writes `capabilityExists && teacherSaidYes`, and the Python's own default is a fallback that should never be the thing deciding.

firstDeployMarkers.note: How each app knows whether a section has EVER been deployed to where it is going now. `deploy.py` writes a marker the first time a section goes out, and the apps read it to decide whether a deploy would ask a question — which is what makes a scheduled deploy safe or a 06:30 failure.

paths.why: A folder deploy asks nothing, so it keeps no marker and counts as always-deployed.

releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.name: section<N>.previous-yyyy-MM-dd_HHmmss.json, beside the marker it replaces
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.legacyName: .netlify_site.previous-yyyy-MM-dd_HHmmss.json, for the older marker that deploy.py still reads and migrates back into the stable path — in the BUILT OUTPUT, never beside the teacher's pages. WHERE THE BUILT OUTPUT IS DIFFERS BY PLATFORM, and getting that wrong is the easy mistake in both directions: <CODE>/.merged_output/section<N>/ on macOS, but %LOCALAPPDATA%\Plantoir\builds\<folder id>\<CODE>\section<N>\ on Windows, because merged_output_root() returns PLANTOIR_BUILD_ROOT/<CODE> with no .merged_output level whenever that variable is set and deploy.ps1 sets it unconditionally. An app that releases only the OTHER platform's spelling releases a path that has never held a marker, so the release does nothing at all and the section goes on publishing over last year's site. Both are attempted on Windows, guarded by existence, so a folder carried across from a mac is covered too.
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.rule: Cutting a section loose from last year's website RENAMES its marker aside, never deletes it, and does so for EVERY destination type rather than only the one the course is configured for now.
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.why: Renamed rather than deleted because the file holds the site's id and its admin address, and a teacher who decides they wanted last year's website after all has no other way back to it. Every destination rather than the primary one because markers are keyed purely by destination TYPE and a course can carry additional targets, so releasing only the primary leaves an additional destination still overwriting last year's site. The name is frozen and shared so a teacher is told the same filename whichever app they are sitting at.
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.windowsOwes: ✅ Done 2026-09-08 (GitHub issues #66 and #69, GUI-IMPROVEMENTS.md row 458). Both halves are fixed and both were real: AssistWorkspace.ReleaseSite returned INSIDE the first folder that held a marker, so a section pinned to both Netlify and Cloudflare kept publishing over last year's Cloudflare site; and it did not know the legacy path. It now walks every destination in one undo transaction, returns a record that keeps "still pinned" apart from "there was nothing to release", and releases the legacy marker at BOTH spellings above. Kept in place rather than deleted, so this block reads as the history of a fixed defect rather than as an outstanding one.
releasedWhenASectionRollsOver.safeBecause: deploy.py and build_site.py build exact marker paths and never glob the folder, so a .previous-*.json sitting beside them is inert.

firstDeployMarkers.rule: Read the marker for the destination the course is configured for NOW — not any marker, and not the other one.
firstDeployMarkers.why: A course deployed to Netlify and then switched to Cloudflare has NEVER been deployed to Cloudflare, and its first Cloudflare deploy will ask what to call the site. Treating the old Netlify marker as proof schedules exactly the deploy that stops at a prompt at half six with nobody there — the failure the 'never been deployed' refusal exists to prevent.

note: The two files both apps WRITE, and the Python then reads. Everything else in these contracts describes behaviour; this describes a format, and a format that drifts corrupts a teacher's course quietly. Both spellings below have already caused a real bug: `SectionAdder` was found writing the OLD frontmatter key on both platforms, so a section added through the app was born in a schema everything else had moved off, and the TEST agreed with the code.

pageVisibility.note: Frontmatter. Whether students see a page — the single most consequential field in the product, since getting it backwards publishes something a teacher held back. TWO spellings exist and both must be read: `publish:` (current) and `draft:` (legacy, meaning the OPPOSITE). Course-level pages carry a key per section instead.

readingCases.why: The legacy key means the opposite. Reading it as-is publishes a page the teacher hid.
A page that says nothing is VISIBLE — that is Quartz's own default, and changing it here would hide every page written before the field existed.

writingCases.note: The runnable half of `writingRules` above — give `before` to the writer, ask it for `setVisible`, and expect `after` and `expectChanged` exactly. `before` and `after` are WHOLE files, newline for newline, not the frontmatter fragments `readingCases` uses. Deliberately inside the subset both apps handle identically: LF endings, no inline `# comment` after a value (macOS rewrites the line and drops one, Windows preserves it — a real difference, and not one this list is the place to settle), no indented keys, and no blank line before the opening fence.

cases.after:
---
title: Day one
publishForSection1: true
---
Body.
cases.before:
---
title: Day one
draftSection1: true
---
Body.
cases.why: The per-section spelling on a course-level page: the new key takes the old key's own line, so the teacher's frontmatter keeps its order and the diff is one line.

cases.after:
---
title: Day one
publish: true
---
Body.
cases.before:
---
title: Day one
draft: true
---
Body.
cases.why: The plain spelling, on a page inside a section's own folder. Same migration, and note the polarity flips: `draft: true` and `publish: true` are opposites.

A page carrying BOTH spellings loses the legacy one. Leaving it would leave a line saying the opposite of the line above it, which the next reader — or the next build of an older toolchain — could believe.

Already saying the right thing, still spelled the old way: migrated anyway, once. This is the exception `migrationIsTheOneExceptionToRule4` describes — a page nobody ever flips is exactly the page that would keep its legacy key forever.
And once migrated, rule 4 holds again: writing the value it already has changes nothing, so the file's modification time is left alone and the next build is not fooled into rebuilding it.
A page with no frontmatter at all gets a block of its own.

cases.after:
---
publish: false
title: Day one
---
Body.
cases.why: A block with neither spelling in it: the key is inserted straight after the opening fence — ABOVE `title`, which is where the course installer puts it too and which can never land inside a nested list or a block scalar. A migration keeps its line; only a key being added for the first time moves to the top.

writingRules.detail: Publishing a `draftSection1: true` page writes `publishForSection1: true` on the SAME line, and the `draftSection1` line is gone; a page carrying BOTH spellings loses the legacy one. The new key takes the old key's position, so a migrated page shows a one-line diff in Obsidian rather than reordered frontmatter.
writingRules.rule: A page written in the old spelling is MIGRATED to the new key, and the legacy key removed, the first time something edits its visibility
writingRules.why: Decided 2026-09-07 (Russell), replacing the rule this list carried since it was written — 'a page written in the old spelling KEEPS it, inverted' — which the mac implemented and Windows never did. Migration leaves a teacher's file in one current spelling rather than two competing ones, stops the old key accumulating forever, and is what documentation/04-course-setup.md and 08-course-config-reference.md have described all along. There is no flag day: the build reads both spellings, so a legacy course builds exactly as before and converts one page at a time. Rejected: keeping the old key inverted (the mac's behaviour until it adopts this) — it would make both documentation files wrong and leave teachers' pages carrying a legacy key indefinitely; and leaving the divergence recorded but unresolved, which is how a knownDivergence becomes permanent.
writingRules.migrationIsTheOneExceptionToRule4: A legacy page whose value is already right is still rewritten, once, to migrate the key — although 'writing the value it already has changes nothing' says a no-op write must not touch the file. Deliberate, and it is a property of the WRITER rather than something either app's plan produces today: both plan layers drop a page whose visibility already matches into their 'already right' list and never write it, so nothing currently asks for this write. It is pinned anyway because the day something does — a sweep, a repair, a tool that sets rather than toggles — the cost is one page's modification time moving once, and it buys a course that converges on one spelling instead of carrying legacy keys on exactly the pages nobody ever flips. A rule that migrated only on a genuine change would leave those pages old forever. (This sentence said 'reachable only inside a batch that is changing OTHER pages' until 2026-09-09, when implementing it on the mac showed that a batch skips such a page too — corrected rather than deleted, so nobody goes looking again for the code path it described.)

writingRules.rule: Edit the LINE, never round-trip the YAML
writingRules.why: A YAML library reorders keys and strips comments. The frontmatter is the teacher's, and they will see the diff in Obsidian.

writingRules.rule: A page with no frontmatter at all gets a block of its own

writingRules.detail: Report 'no change' rather than rewriting the file. One exception, on purpose: a legacy-spelled page is migrated even when its value is already right — see the first rule.
writingRules.rule: Writing the value it already has changes nothing
writingRules.why: A no-op write still updates the modification time, which makes the next build think the content changed.

fields.why: Which section these dates belong to. Both apps have always WRITTEN it and this list did not name it until 2026-09-06, when wiring the list into the Windows suite turned it up — a field carried by two apps and described by nobody is one a third reader would drop. It is redundant with the file's own name, which is why nothing broke: the mac reads it with the filename's section as the fallback, and Windows does not read it at all. Keep writing it — a timetable copied out of its folder, or attached to a problem report, still says what it is for.
Plain dates, not a recurrence rule. A school timetable has holidays, PA days and the week the schedule turned inside out for exams — no rule survives contact with it.

Where the dates came from, IN THE TEACHER'S OWN WORDS — 'timetable.xlsx, block H'. It is what they read months later when they wonder where these came from, and 'a Google Sheet' answers that far less well than they can themselves. Read back as 'not recorded' when absent rather than blank.
When they were written down, so a teacher can tell a timetable from last semester.

sectionTimetable.note: `courses/<CODE>/.internal/timetable/section<N>.json` — the dates a section actually meets, written down once by whichever app the teacher used and read by both. It lives INSIDE the course folder so it travels with a backup, an archive and a restore; a teacher who restores a course gets its timetable back with it.
sectionTimetable.verified: Both apps use this exact path — mac `SectionTimetable`, Windows `TimetableMemory.cs`.
